name: Tetracosactide
lead: Tetracosactide, also called cosyntropin or ACTH 1-24, is a synthetic peptide made of the first 24 of the 39 amino acids of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH). It keeps the full activity of the parent hormone and prompts the adrenal glands to release cortisol, which is why its main use is the ACTH (Synacthen) stimulation test of adrenal function.[1][2]

The link to appearance runs through cortisol balance. Cortisol status affects energy, appetite, body weight and body composition, and the stimulation test is how clinicians identify adrenal insufficiency, whose symptoms include fatigue, appetite loss and weight loss, along with other adrenal and pituitary conditions that change how a person looks.[3][4] In recovery-oriented forum discussion, people who have used anabolic steroids or other hormones mention the cosyntropin test as a way to find out whether the adrenal axis responds.[11][12]

Brand names include Synacthen, Synacthen Depot, Cortrosyn and Nuvacthen. In the United States the synthetic form carries a diagnostic-only label, while in the United Kingdom tetracosactide has also been used therapeutically in some settings.[1][2]

quick.overview:
Tetracosactide is a lab-made version of the first 24 amino acids of ACTH, the pituitary hormone that signals the adrenals to make cortisol. It is mostly used as a diagnostic injection.

By showing whether the adrenal glands respond, it helps identify adrenal insufficiency, a cause of fatigue and weight loss that people link to how they look and feel.
quick.mechanism: It binds ACTH receptors on the adrenal cortex and triggers cortisol release. A healthy adrenal gland raises blood cortisol within about 30 minutes of injection, which lets clinicians separate adrenal from pituitary causes of deficiency.[1]
quick.risks: Therapeutic ACTH products can raise infection risk, suppress the HPA axis and cause Cushing-like effects; hypersensitivity is a contraindication.[1] It is a prescription medicine; in the UK it has also been used short-term when glucocorticoids are unsuitable.

paras: The cosyntropin stimulation test is used to diagnose primary and secondary adrenal insufficiency, including glucocorticoid-induced adrenal insufficiency, and to confirm non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia.[1][3][5] It is also used as an alternative to the insulin tolerance test in corticotroph deficiency, although its sensitivity is not optimal for partial deficits.[6] In a healthy person a single injection raises blood cortisol within about 30 minutes, and a result in the range of 18 to 20 micrograms per decilitre is commonly used as a normal response, with cut-offs varying by assay.[1][13]

The UK product label also covers short-term therapeutic use where glucocorticoids would normally be used but are unsuitable, such as some cases of colitis or rheumatoid arthritis. Animal-derived corticotropin (a different product) is used for infantile spasms, acute multiple sclerosis relapses and several inflammatory conditions.[1]

Adrenal insufficiency can bring weight loss, fatigue and skin changes, while cortisol excess brings central weight gain and facial rounding, so the test is a first step toward finding and correcting a cortisol imbalance.[3][4] The peptide itself is not used cosmetically.

Human studies cover diagnostic testing of adrenal function in primary and secondary adrenal insufficiency, cirrhosis, septic shock and critical illness, and none examine appearance outcomes.[3][8][14][15]

A randomized trial group compared cosyntropin, vigabatrin and combined therapy in infantile spasms, and the earlier ICISS trial tested hormonal treatment with or without vigabatrin.[7][16] A study of residual corticosteroid production in autoimmune Addison disease used cosyntropin stimulation to measure it.[8]

Methods research has examined whether the subcutaneous route and a nasal tetracosactide formulation can stand in for intravenous or intramuscular injection in the short Synacthen test, and a withdrawn registered trial planned to compare intramuscular and intravenous testing in healthy volunteers.[17][18][19] Registered studies also examine adrenal insufficiency in cirrhosis, in children after cardiac surgery and in postural tachycardia syndrome.[20][21]

Increased infection risk, suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and Cushing's syndrome are listed risks for ACTH medications, and contraindications vary by country.[1] The US label advises caution about live vaccines during immunosuppressive use of corticotropin.[1][2]

In normal physiology the pituitary releases ACTH, which stimulates the adrenal cortex to produce glucocorticoids; cortisol then signals back to the hypothalamus to shut the cycle off.[1] Tetracosactide binds the same melanocortin 2 receptor target on adrenal cells as full-length ACTH.[1] Its ability to provoke cortisol release in someone whose adrenals are functional, but not in someone whose adrenals are damaged or atrophied, is the basis of the test.[3][4]

Animal-derived corticotropin products were first approved in the United States from 1950, and a synthetic version was created as a replacement for them.[1] Cortrosyn was approved by the FDA in 1970, and UK Synacthen formulations were approved in 2008; ownership of these products has changed hands several times.[1] ACTH products have drawn attention for steep price increases and, in 2007, for media reports of tetracosactide being used as a performance-enhancing drug by professional cyclists.[1]

Cosyntropin is prescription-only.[1][2] On T Nation testosterone-treatment threads, posters recommend an ACTH stimulation test to evaluate adrenal function, and some users argue that passing the test shows the adrenals can produce cortisol under stress without proving their baseline output is adequate.[11][12]
